item.title: Weakened association between sequential phenological events corresponds to interphase extension
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-79161-w

Seasonal events in temperate deciduous trees, from leaf-out to leaf fall, follow a fixed annual sequence. This study shows that the timing of consecutive events is statistically associated in European trees, but that the association between fruiting and leaf coloration has weakened in some species as the interval between these phases has increased.

item.title: Hydrogen-bond-mediated quasi-two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks for ultrahigh gold extraction
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78532-7

Covalent organic frameworks are ideal for precious metal recovery but the confinement of binding sites within inner pores often leads to restricted mass transfer and limits extraction capacities. Here, the authors report a quasi-2D topology-directed strategy to construct exposed binding sites for highly efficient gold recovery.

item.title: A combinatorial genetics approach reveals limits to redundancy within Plasmodium falciparum invasion ligand families
item.content:encoded:
Nature Communications, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41467-026-78985-w

The authors use a genetic approach to explore redundancy within two multigene families important for Plasmodium falciparum invasion of human red blood cells, revealing that not all family members function equivalently.

item.title: CryoET imaging reveals that mitotic spindles are locally organized by microtubule density and Eg5 activity
item.description:
William Conway, Daija Bobe, Vitaly Zimyanin, Gunar Fabig, Alex de Marco, Stefanie Redemann
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78938-3
Abstract When eukaryotic cells divide, a mitotic spindle, composed of microtubule filaments interacting with molecular motors, self-assembles and is responsible for aligning and segregating chromosomes to the opposite daughter cells. Recent structural studies revealed that spindles are composed of short microtubules that do not span the full pole-to-chromosome distance. It remains unclear how these short, disconnected microtubules collectively assemble a bipolar spindle. Using cryo-electron tomography to map microtubule polarity in human spindles, we find that microtubules organize with consistent 8 nm wall-to-wall spacing. Spacing scales inversely with local microtubule density, consistent with organization by density-driven steric interactions, analogous to liquid crystal ordering. We find that the Eg5 motor establishes local antiparallel overlap independently of spindle bipolarity, while a balance of Eg5 and dynein regulates microtubule density to maintain spindle architecture. Together, these findings reveal the mesoscale principles by which cells build complex, self-healing cellular architectures from nanoscale building blocks.

item.title: Antimicrobial peptides derived from Nemuri induce ribosomal condensation to inhibit translation
item.description:
Suguru Nishinami, Moynul Hasan, Tatsuya Niwa, Tomohiro Inui, Takeshi Yokoyama, Hiroto Otsuki, Yuta Ogasawara, Hiroka Sugai, et al.
Nature Communications, vol. 17, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78960-5
Abstract Antibiotic resistance is a global health threat requiring antimicrobials with alternative modes of action. Growing evidence indicates that bacteria organize key intracellular processes through biomolecular condensates and other forms of spatial organization, yet whether such spatial organization can be exploited as an antimicrobial target remains unclear. Here, we identify intrinsically disordered antimicrobial peptides, generated from the Drosophila sleep-inducing protein Nemuri, that inhibit bacterial growth by targeting ribosomal organization. Mechanistically, these peptides enter bacterial cells without overt membrane disruption and accumulate in ribosome-rich regions, where they bind broadly to RNA and ribosomal surfaces through multivalent interactions. This engagement remodels ribosome-rich regions into condensates with reduced ribosomal mobility, thereby suppressing global protein synthesis and distinguishing these peptides from canonical site-specific ribosome-targeting antibiotics. Furthermore, Nemuri-derived peptides exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, including activity against drug-resistant pathogens, with low cytotoxicity toward Drosophila and mammalian cells. Together, our findings identify the organization and material dynamics of bacterial ribosomes as a biophysical vulnerability that can be exploited by antimicrobial peptides, revealing how a naturally evolved metazoan host-defense system turns intracellular organization itself into an antibacterial target.

item.title: Widespread selection of antibiotic resistance within hospital sewers
item.description:
Declan A. Gray, Nguyen Thi Nhung, Roelof Dirk Coertze, Mutshiene Deogratias Ekwanzala, Noel Waters, Josef D. Järhult, Michaela Wenzel, Christina Åhrén, et al.
Nature Communications, vol. 17, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78836-8
Abstract Environmental microbiomes are sources of diverse antibiotic resistance determinants that can be mobilized and transferred to human pathogens under a selection pressure from antibiotics. Hospital sewers contain more antibiotics than most environments and are thus increasingly recognised as potential arenas for resistance evolution. However, it is unknown if resistance selection occurs there and what the drivers are. Here we show selection of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within Swedish hospital sewers. Evidence include; consistent selection of multiple resistances in Escherichia coli exposed to filtered wastewater from ten hospitals, but not to corresponding municipal wastewaters; in-situ enrichment of resistant over sensitive E. coli from wastewater to sewer biofilms at hospitals, but not at municipal sites; and higher resistance in bacteria collected from hospital sewers than from municipal sites as assessed by culturing and metagenomics. Evidence for drivers includes complete rescue of sensitive E. coli by addition of resistance genes to fluoroquinolones and β-lactams, and cellular effects typical for β-lactams. Measured concentrations by liquid-chromatography-tandem-mass-spectrometry compared to selective thresholds identify ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime as principal selective agents. Antibiotic concentrations and use data allow extrapolation of risks beyond Sweden. Given the absence of detectable selection at municipal sites, mitigations of risks in hospital sewers should be prioritized.

item.title: Resolving the Kay–Dunn limit and the speed–endurance dilemma in ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 for DRAM-class sub-volt capacitors
item.description:
Geun Hyeong Park, Sanghyun Jo, Sungwook Park, Yong Hyeon Cho, Hyeong Seok Choi, Hyun Woo Jeong, Se Hyun Kim, Dong Hyun Lee, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78705-4
Abstract Ferroelectric hafnium zirconium oxide can increase charge density in scaled capacitors, but its high coercive field limits the low-voltage, high endurance switching required for dynamic random-access memory and embedded ferroelectric memories. Here we show that plasma-engineered (111)-textured TiN electrodes with N-rich, oxidation-resistant surfaces suppress interfacial oxidation and enable robust switching in 5 nm Hf 0.5 Zr 0.5 O 2 capacitors. The devices exhibit saturated hysteresis at 0.6 V, with 2 P r = 31.5 μC cm −2 and E c = 0.62 MV cm −1 , and no hard electrical breakdown through 10 12 bipolar cycles. Their nucleation-limited switching kinetics extrapolate to sub-nanosecond polarisation reversal at DRAM-relevant capacitor areas. At 1.1 V, circuit simulations of a common plate 1T–1 C cell yield short- and long-term stand-by sensing margins of 482 and 201 mV under a 20 fF bit line load. Electrode texture and interface engineering therefore enable low-voltage, high speed switching without compromising endurance, mitigating the practical Kay–Dunn scaling penalty and the speed–endurance dilemma.

item.title: Exaiptasia diaphana core microbiome members are lost under climate change conditions despite host thermal tolerance
item.description:
Kaden Muffett, Stephen Williams, Sophia MacVittie, Mara JW Schwiesow, Susan Arechiga Mendoza, Salma Arechiga Mendoza, Hailey Hatch-West, E. Maggie Sogin
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79034-2
Abstract Acute and chronic exposure to elevated temperatures associated with Global Climate Change (GCC) threatens the structure and function of host-associated microbiomes, yet predicting microbial responses to heat stress remains challenging. We exposed two lines of the sea anemone, Exaiptasia diaphana , to acute and chronic thermal stress to quantify the impacts on cnidarian physiology and microbiome composition. Acute exposure caused rapid algal bleaching that was paired with pronounced shifts in bacteriome structure in both lines within 14 days of thermal exposure. Chronic exposure significantly affected the population structure, photo-physiology and bacteriome composition in only one host line, suggesting acclimation capacity depends on host-algal genetic backgrounds. Using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing of 493 individuals sampled across 180 days, we found that sampling date explained nine-fold more variation in the microbiome composition than temperature exposure. Despite this temporal variation, we identified 16 indicator taxa that consistently changed in relative abundance under thermal stress. These taxa became central hubs in microbial association networks with increasing levels of thermal stress, suggesting they played key roles in bacteriome reorganization. As many of these taxa were present in other cnidarians, including reef-building corals, they may represent targets for conservation strategies that aim to enhance resilience on reefs.

item.title: LytU is a bridge-link isopeptidase that contributes to vancomycin resistance in Staphylococcus aureus
item.description:
Lina Antenucci, Chandan Thapa, Salla Virtanen, Timo A. Lehti, Annsy Arredondo, Ilona Pitkänen, Benita Westerlund-Wikström, Helena Tossavainen, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78872-4
Abstract Emergence of antimicrobial resistance is a pressing global issue. Although myriads of mechanisms for survival against antimicrobial pressure have surfaced, one key strategy is the structural modification of peptidoglycan, the main defense line in Gram-positive bacteria e.g., notorious pathogen Staphylococcus aureus . Here we show that the recently identified peptidoglycan hydrolase (PGH) LytU is an unusual catalyst in the lysostaphin (M23B) family of zinc-endopeptidases that hydrolyze the glycyl-glycine peptide bond in S. aureus . Unlike any other PGH recognized thus far, LytU hydrolyzes the isopeptide bond between the lysine ε amino group and pentaglycine, thus functioning as a bridge-link hydrolase. We discovered that LytM and LytU are functionally non-redundant, and they contribute to the cell wall remodeling at different stages of PG maturation. Additionally, we demonstrate that LytU particularly targets the PG precursor, pGly-Lipid II, and its overexpression leads to growth inhibition and a less densely cross-linked cell wall, which increases susceptibility to lysostaphin. Interestingly, LytU expression enhances resistance to the glycopeptide vancomycin, the drug of last resort against S. aureus .

item.title: Retarding efficiency loss upon scaling in perovskite photovoltaics as fill factor becomes the bottleneck
item.description:
Buyi Yan, Ruihao Gong, Yanchun Huang, Nannan Gu, Runfeng Li, Dongxue Liu, Kangrong Yan, Xuehui Xu, et al.
Nature Communications
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-78867-1
Abstract Perovskite solar cells approach crystalline-silicon efficiencies at small areas, yet substantial performance losses during scale-up hinder their translation into practical modules. Here we quantify the contributions of device-performance parameters to efficiency loss during scale-up across diverse perovskite technologies, identifying fill factor ( $${FF}$$ F F ) as a major contributor and target for mitigating this loss. Further analysis resolves the FF deficit into voltage-, diode-non-ideality- and transport-associated contributions. Cryo-controlled processing provides an experimental route to preserve $${FF}$$ F F by regulating intermediate-phase evolution during crystallization. The resulting $${FF}$$ F F -preservation advantage arises predominantly from reduced diode non-ideality, with the other contributions being smaller. This advantage increases across device scales. A mini-module (19.48 cm 2 aperture) achieves a record certified steady-state efficiency of 23.9% with an $${FF}$$ F F of 83.3%, the highest reported for perovskite modules. The same $${FF}$$ F F limitation governs operational performance decay, linking efficiency retention during scale-up with long-term stability. Together, these results establish $${FF}$$ F F preservation and the factors governing it as central to mitigating performance loss during scale-up and operation.

item.title: Ketene as a gas phase intermediate in acetic acid ketonization on TiO2
item.description:
Jiayan Xu, William JI DeBenedetti, Xingyu Wang, Yiqing Wu, Libor Kovarik, Christopher R. O’Connor, Feng Gao, Janos Szanyi, et al.
Nature Communications, vol. 17, issue 1
DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77945-8
Abstract Reactive gas-phase intermediates are often underappreciated in heterogeneous catalysis, despite their potential to control key catalytic steps. Here, we provide direct experimental evidence that ketene can act as an intermediate in acetic acid ketonization, a mechanism that has long been debated. Using faceted TiO 2 (101) nanoparticles assembled into layers of controlled thickness, we show that ketene, formed from surface acetate, migrates through interparticle voids via desorption-readsorption events before reacting with surface acetate to yield acetone. Surface science and reactor studies reveal a direct correlation between ketene and acetone production and the depth to which the particle layers are saturated. Ab initio calculations support ketene’s reactivity via low-barrier coupling pathways that converge on a common β-ketoacid intermediate. Here, we show that ketene can act as a mobile gas-phase intermediate and underscore the broader importance of spatially decoupled elementary steps in determining reactivity and selectivity in catalytic systems.
